lesson.title: The Single Highest Point: Defining the Global Maximum
lesson.summary: A global, or absolute, maximum is the single largest value a function attains anywhere on its domain, and it can occur at an endpoint, an interior turning point, or at several locations at once.
lesson.body:
A function has a global maximum at x = c if f(c) is greater than or equal to f(x) for every single x in the domain of f, with no exceptions anywhere. The value f(c) itself is called the global maximum value, or the absolute maximum value. This is a strong requirement: f(c) has to outperform every other output the function ever produces, not just the outputs nearby. That distinction, everywhere versus nearby, is what will separate a global maximum from a local maximum in the next couple of sections.

The Extreme Value Theorem tells you a global maximum exists, when f is continuous on a closed interval, but it does not tell you where it lives. In practice there are only a limited number of places it could be hiding: the two endpoints of the interval, and any interior points where the function stops rising and starts falling, the kind of interior turning point previewed in the last two sections. Checking all of these candidates and comparing their output values is the standard search strategy.

Work through f(x) = x^3 - 3x on the closed interval [-2, 2]. This is a polynomial, so it is continuous, and the interval is closed and bounded, so a global maximum is guaranteed to exist. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3, and the tangent line is horizontal exactly where f'(x) = 0, that is where 3x^2 = 3, so x^2 = 1, giving x = -1 and x = 1. Both of these interior candidates fall inside [-2, 2], so along with the two endpoints there are four candidates in total to check: x = -2, -1, 1, and 2.

Evaluate f at all four: f(-2) = (-2)^3 - 3(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2. f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2. f(1) = 1^3 - 3(1) = 1 - 3 = -2. f(2) = 2^3 - 3(2) = 8 - 6 = 2. The four candidate values are -2, 2, -2, and 2. The largest of these is 2, and it happens twice, once at the interior point x = -1 and once at the endpoint x = 2. So the global maximum value of f on [-2, 2] is 2, attained at both x = -1 and x = 2.

This example illustrates two things worth remembering. First, a global maximum can occur at an interior point, at an endpoint, or, as happened here, tied at more than one location simultaneously; nothing in the definition forbids ties. Second, finding it required checking every candidate and comparing actual output values, guessing from the shape of the graph is not reliable enough on its own.
